name: Plain-sawn (flat-sawn)
process: The log is sawn through and through, so most boards have their growth rings roughly parallel to the face, in arches. The face is tangential: the rings cut obliquely give the arched 'cathedral' figure, and the width is as wide as the log allows. It yields the most timber and moves most across its width.

ringAngleToFace.text: Rings roughly parallel to the face, usually in arches; below the rift range (under about 45 degrees).
ringAngleToFace.source: WOODWEB Knowledge Base, 'Rays and Flecks in Oak' (forum digest of 30 September 2009; answer by Gene Wengert), https://woodweb.com/knowledge_base/Rays_and_Flecks_in_Oak.html ; Wikipedia, 'Quarter sawing', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_sawing (read 2026-09-26)

widthShrinkageOak.source: Meier, E. The Wood Database: English Oak (Quercus robur), https://www.wood-database.com/english-oak/ (read 2026-09-26)

cupping.text: A flatsawn board cups more than a quartersawn one.

surface.figure: Arched cathedrals and wide bands of earlywood pores; no ray fleck (the rays are cut end-on as short dark lines).

photograph: Arched figure repeating up each board; wider boards; each board a different pattern.
